[[Nigerian Chieftaincy|Chief]] '''Cyprian Odiatu Duaka Ekwensi''' {{Audio|LL-Q1860 (eng)-Chikeme Chizurum-Cyprian Ekwensi.wav|Listen|help=no}} {{post-nominals|country=NG|MFR}}<ref name=dt>{{cite news|title=Cyprian Ekwensi dies at 86|url= http://dailytrust.com/index.php?option=com_content&task=view&id=4253&Itemid=45|date=6 November 2007|access-date=21 November 2007 |newspaper=[[Daily Trust]]}}</ref> (26 September 1921 – 4 November 2007) was a [[Nigerian literature|Nigerian]] author of novels, short stories, and [[children's books]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Cyprian Ekwensi {{!}} Nigerian Author {{!}} Novels, Children's Books, & Other Short Stories |url=https://cyprainekwensi.com/ |access-date=2026-03-15 |website=cyprainekwensi.com}}</ref>

==Biography==

===Early life, education and family===
Cyprian Odiatu Duaka Ekwensi, an [[Igbo people|Igbo]], was born in [[Minna]], the capital city of [[Niger State]], north-central Nigeria.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2021-12-01 |title=Nigeria Today Is Like A Yarn By Cyprian Ekwensi - |url=https://thenewsnigeria.com.ng/2021/12/01/nigeria-today-is-like-a-yarn-by-cyprian-ekwensi/ |access-date=2022-03-06 |website=The NEWS}}</ref> He was a native of Nkwelle Ezunaka in [[Oyi]] local government area, [[Anambra State]], southeastern [[Nigeria]]. His father was David Anadumaka, a storyteller and elephant hunter.<ref name=nb>{{cite news|first= Shola|last= Adenekan|title=Prolific Writer Who Chronicled Modern Life in West Africa|url=http://www.thenewblackmagazine.com/view.aspx?index=1073|work=The New Black Magazine online|date=11 November 2007|access-date=21 November 2007 }}</ref>

Ekwensi attended [[Government College, Umuahia|Government College]] in [[Umuahia]], [[Abia State]] in southeast Nigeria, [[Achimota College]] in [[Ghana]], and the [[School of Forestry, Ibadan]], after which he worked for two years as a forestry officer.<ref name="dt" /> He also studied [[pharmacy]] at [[Yaba Technical Institute]], [[Lagos School of Pharmacy]], and the [[Chelsea School of Pharmacy]] of the [[University of London]]. He taught at [[Igbobi College]].<ref name=dt/>

Ekwensi married Eunice Anyiwo, and they had five children.<ref name=dt/> He has many grandchildren, including his son Cyprian Ikechi Ekwensi, who is named after his grandfather, and his oldest grandchild Adrianne Tobechi Ekwensi.

===Governmental career===
Ekwensi was employed as Head of Features at the [[Nigerian Broadcasting Corporation]] (NBC) and by the [[Federal Ministry of Information and Culture (Nigeria)|Ministry of Information]] during the [[Nigerian First Republic|First Republic]];<ref>{{cite book|last=Gérard|first= Albert S.|title= European-Language Writing in Sub-Saharan Africa|year=1986|publisher=John Benjamins Publishing Company|isbn= 963-05-3834-2|page=654}}</ref> he eventually became Director of the latter.<ref name=nb /> He resigned his position in 1966, before the [[Nigerian Civil War|Civil War]], and defected to Enugu with his family. He later served as chair of the Bureau for External Publicity of [[Biafra]],<ref>{{cite encyclopedia|title =Cyprian Ekwensi|encyclopedia=Encyclopedia of World Biography|publisher=[[Thomson Gale]]|url=http://www.bookrags.com/biography/cyprian-ekwensi/}}</ref> prior to its reabsorption by Nigeria.

===Literary career===
Ekwensi wrote hundreds of short stories (his story "Law of the  Grazing Field" was included in ''An African Treasury'', a 1960 anthology edited by [[Langston Hughes]]),<ref>{{cite news|url=https://archive.nytimes.com/www.nytimes.com/books/01/04/22/specials/hughes-treasury.html|title=Literary Lights From the Dark Continent|first=Milton|last=Bracker|newspaper=[[The New York Times]]|date=18 September 1960|access-date=7 February 2026}}</ref> radio and television [[screenplay|scripts]], and several dozen novels, including children's books.<ref name=dt/> His 1954 ''[[People of the City]]'' was his first book to garner international attention.<ref name=nb/>
His novel ''Drummer Boy'' (1960), based on the life of [[Kokoro (musician)|Benjamin "Kokoro"' Aderounmu]], was a perceptive and powerful description of the wandering, homeless and poverty-stricken life of a street artist.<ref>{{Cite news |title = Authors convention begins in Minna |date = 29 October 2009 |author = CHUKA NNABUIFE |publisher = Nigerian Compass }}</ref> Ekwensi's most successful novel was ''[[Jagua Nana]]'' (1961),<ref>{{cite encyclopedia|year=2003|title = Ekwensi, Cyprian|encyclopedia=Africana: The Encyclopedia of the African and African American Experience|pages=226–227|publisher= Running Press|isbn=0-7624-1642-4 }}</ref> about a [[Nigerian Pidgin English|Pidgin]]-speaking Nigerian woman who leaves her husband to work as a prostitute in a city and falls in love with a teacher.<ref>Gérard, p. 656.</ref> Ekwensi also wrote a sequel to this, ''Jagua Nana's Daughter''.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://msupress.msu.edu/bookTemplate.php?bookID=1135|title=Jagua Nana's Daughter|access-date=21 November 2007|publisher=Michigan State University Press|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070510140350/http://msupress.msu.edu/bookTemplate.php?bookID=1135|archive-date=10 May 2007|df=dmy-all}}</ref>

In 1968, he received the [[Dag Hammarskjöld]] International Prize in Literature.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Nigeria |first=Guardian |date=2018-09-24 |title=Remebering Cyprian Ekwensi And His Phenomenal Works |url=https://guardian.ng/life/748052/ |location=Lagos, Nigeria|access-date=2026-03-15 |newspaper=[[The Guardian (Nigeria)|The Guardian]]|language=en-GB}}</ref> In 2001, he was appointed an [[Orders, decorations, and medals of Nigeria|MFR]] and in 2006, he became a fellow of the [[Nigerian Academy of Letters]].<ref name=dt/>

===Death===
Ekwensi died on 4 November 2007, aged 86, at the Niger Foundation in [[Enugu (city)|Enugu]], where he had undergone an operation for an undisclosed ailment.<ref name=dt/> The [[Association of Nigerian Authors]] (ANA), having intended to present him with an award on 16 November 2007, converted the honour to a posthumous award.<ref>
{{cite news|title=ANA plans post humous award for Ekwensi|url=http://www.thetidenews.com/article.aspx?qrDate=11/11/2007&qrTitle=ANA%20plans%20post%20humous%20award%20for%20Ekwensi&qrColumn=SOUTH%20EAST|location=Port Harcourt, Nigeria|date=11 November 2007|access-date=21 November 2007|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110717042401/http://www.thetidenews.com/article.aspx?qrDate=11%2F11%2F2007&qrTitle=ANA%20plans%20post%20humous%20award%20for%20Ekwensi&qrColumn=SOUTH%20EAST|archive-date=17 July 2011|url-status=dead|df=dmy-all|newspaper=[[The Tide (Nigeria)|The Tide]]}}
</ref>
